$comment: The content backlog. The publish workflow takes the first topic with
status 'pending', generates it, verifies it, publishes it, and marks it
'published'. When the list runs dry the workflow exits cleanly and does
nothing — an empty queue is never an error.
Order matters. The first eight entries are the SEO cluster: a pillar page
and the ASI risk pages that nobody currently owns in search. Everything
after that is supporting and opinion content.
Add topics whenever. 'type: corpus' topics are regenerated from fresh scan
data and can legitimately be repeated each quarter.

topics.title: The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, explained for engineers
topics.brief: The hub page for the whole cluster. Walk all ten ASI categories at a level an engineer can act on: what each one is, one sentence on what it looks like in code, and a link to the deep-dive page for it. Explain how the agentic list differs from the LLM Top 10 and why a separate list was needed at all — the LLM list is about the model, the agentic list is about what happens when the model can act. Be explicit that this is a reference document, not a certification scheme.
structure: Why a separate list from the LLM Top 10 exists
The ten categories, one section each, with a code-level tell for each
Which of these an ordinary SAST tool can and cannot see
How to run an assessment against the list today

topics.title: ASI05: when your agent builds a shell command out of model output
topics.brief: The most viscerally understandable risk in the list, and therefore the best entry point for the cluster. Show a tool handler that interpolates a model-supplied argument into exec(). Show why the usual defences (input validation on the user prompt) do not help, because the dangerous string arrives from the model, not the user. Cover sandboxing, argument arrays instead of shell strings, and allowlisting. Explain how a static scanner can see this and what it will miss.

topics.title: ASI01: agent goal hijack is not the same thing as prompt injection
topics.brief: Draw the distinction carefully — prompt injection is the mechanism, goal hijack is the outcome, and the outcome is worse when the thing being hijacked has tools. Show untrusted retrieved content being concatenated into a system prompt with no delimiting. Show the delimited version. Cover why delimiting alone is insufficient and what else is needed.

topics.title: ASI09: the approval dialog your agent wrote for itself
topics.keyword: human in the loop ai agent security
topics.brief: The most surprising risk in the list and the strongest single piece of content available. If the model composes the text of the confirmation prompt, the human is approving a description, not an action. Show a confirm() call whose message string comes from the model while the executed action comes from a separate field. Argue that approval UI must be rendered from the structured action, never from model prose. This is the post to write well — it is concrete, unfamiliar, and instantly believable.

topics.title: ASI02: your tool definitions are an attack surface
topics.brief: Tools defined with loose schemas, no per-invocation authorisation, and no allowlist. Show a tool whose parameters are typed as string with no constraints, and what an attacker does with that. Cover schema validation, allowlisting, and per-call authorisation distinct from per-session authorisation.

topics.title: EU AI Act Article 50: what an engineering team actually has to ship
keywords: do i need to disclose my chatbot is ai
topics.brief: Article 50 has been in force since 2 August 2026. Most engineering-facing content on it is written by law firms for legal teams. Write the version an engineer needs: the four sub-obligations, which one applies to a chat interface, which applies to generated media, the December 2026 carve-out for pre-existing generative systems, and the machine-readable marking requirement. Correct the common misreading that the Digital Omnibus moved this deadline — it moved Annex III high-risk obligations to December 2027, not Article 50. Be scrupulous about not implying the tool creates compliance.

topics.title: ASI03: agents inherit your credentials, and they never log out
topics.brief: Long-lived tokens handed to an agent process, no per-task credential exchange, no expiry. Cover why the standard human-session model breaks when the actor is a loop. Short-lived scoped credentials, per-task exchange, and why an agent should never hold the same token across two user contexts.

topics.title: ASI06: the agent remembers what the attacker told it last week
topics.brief: Persistent memory with no tenant scoping, no validation on write, no TTL. Show the multi-tenant leak: user A's injected instruction retrieved into user B's context. Cover scoping keys, write-time validation, and expiry.

topics.title: ASI10: can you stop it?
topics.brief: Two questions almost nothing in the wild answers yes to: is there an audit trail of what the agent did, and is there a way to stop it mid-run. Show an agent loop with no AbortController and no structured action log. Cover what an audit record needs to contain to be useful after an incident.

topics.title: ASI08: the agent loop with no upper bound
topics.brief: Uncapped iteration, unhandled tool errors, and what happens when one failing tool turns into a retry storm across a multi-agent system. Cover iteration caps, circuit breakers, and error containment at the dispatch boundary. Note the cost angle — this is the risk with a monthly invoice attached, which makes it the easiest one to get a finance conversation about.

topics.title: ASI04: npx, unpinned, at runtime
topics.brief: MCP servers launched with npx and no version pin, dependencies floating on caret ranges, no SBOM. Explain why an agent's supply chain is worse than an application's — the agent fetches and executes capabilities at runtime based on configuration, so the dependency set is not fully known at build time.

topics.title: ASI07: two agents talking over plain HTTP
topics.brief: Handoffs between agents with no authentication, no signing, no transport security. Show a handoff payload that any process on the network can forge. Cover message signing, mTLS, and why 'it's internal' stopped being an argument some time ago.

topics.title: I ran three general-purpose SAST tools over an AI agent. Here is what they said.
topics.brief: Take the deliberately-vulnerable reference agent that ships with the product and run general-purpose scanners over it. Report honestly what each one caught and missed. Do not strawman them — they are good tools solving a different problem. The point is that a tool call is not a function call as far as taint analysis is concerned, and that a missing iteration cap is not a vulnerability class any of them model. Be fair; fairness is the credibility.

topics.title: What a scan of the open-source agent ecosystem actually shows
topics.keyword: open source ai agent security study
topics.brief: THE FLAGSHIP PIECE. Report the aggregate findings from the corpus scan: how many repositories, how many files, which rules fire most often, and what that suggests about where the ecosystem's blind spots are. Aggregates only, no naming. Be rigorous about what a static finding is and is not — these are signals requiring human triage, not confirmed vulnerabilities, and framework repositories will legitimately show findings for application-level controls that belong to the caller. Publish the precision figure in the same post. The honesty is the differentiator.

topics.title: The security questionnaire question nobody has an answer to yet
topics.brief: Enterprise buyers have started adding AI-specific rows to vendor questionnaires and most vendors are answering them in prose. Walk through what a defensible answer looks like: a dated assessment against a named framework, a list of what was checked, a list of what was not, and the findings with their disposition. Emphasise that an honest 'we checked these ten categories, here are the four findings and what we did about them' beats a confident 'yes' every single time in a real review.

topics.title: Prompt injection is treated as a model problem. Most of it is a code problem.
topics.brief: The industry response to prompt injection has been overwhelmingly runtime: guardrails, classifiers, filters at the boundary. Argue that a large share of real exposure is decided at the point where a developer writes the string concatenation, and that this is visible in source before anything is deployed. Not a claim that runtime defences are unnecessary — a claim that the code-level layer is currently unexamined.

topics.title: Why I publish this scanner's false-positive rate
topics.brief: Build-in-public piece. Explain the measured precision figure, how it was measured, and why publishing it is a commercial decision rather than a confession. Include a real false positive from the scanner's own output, traced to its root cause — the regex that matched a docstring, the missing word boundary. Engineers trust the vendor who shows them a bug in their own tool.

topics.title: A TODO comment should never make a scanner report you as safe
topics.brief: The design story: rules that look for evidence of a mitigation will happily accept a comment saying the mitigation is planned. Explain the bug, the fix (strip comments before matching control evidence), and the regression test. Short, specific, and the kind of post that gets shared inside engineering teams.

topics.title: A pre-ship checklist for anyone putting an agent in front of customers
topics.brief: A genuinely useful free artefact: the questions to answer before an agent touches production traffic, grouped by the ten ASI categories, phrased as yes/no questions with the failure mode named. Give it away with no gate. This is the piece that earns links.

topics.title: How to review an MCP server before you let an agent load it
topics.brief: MCP servers are the most casually-installed executable dependency in the current stack. Practical review procedure: pin the version, read the tool descriptions as an attack surface, check what filesystem and network access it requests, check whether tool descriptions can be changed server-side after installation.

topics.title: LLM06: the service role key in the agent's environment
topics.brief: Wildcard scopes, admin API keys, GRANT ALL, service-role database keys handed to an agent because scoping them was fiddly. Show what least privilege looks like for a process whose next action is decided by a language model.

topics.title: LLM10: no max_tokens, no timeout, no rate limit
topics.brief: Denial of wallet as a security risk rather than an ops problem. Model calls with no token ceiling, no timeout, no per-user rate limit, in a loop. Cover the three controls and where each belongs.

topics.title: Putting an agent security gate in CI without annoying everybody
topics.brief: Practical piece on wiring a scanner into pull requests: severity thresholds, why failing the build on every finding trains people to ignore it, SARIF upload to the code-scanning tab, and scanning only changed paths on PRs with a full scan weekly.

topics.title: Agent security when there is no security team
topics.keyword: startup ai security no security team
topics.brief: Most teams shipping agents have no AppSec function and will not hire one. What the highest-value hour of work looks like for them, ordered by risk reduced per hour spent. Honest about what a scanner does and does not replace.

topics.title: How to triage a static-analysis finding you do not understand
topics.brief: A short methodology: reproduce the reasoning, decide whether the trigger is real, decide whether the mitigation genuinely exists elsewhere, record the disposition. Emphasise that a recorded, reasoned dismissal is a valid and auditable outcome, and is what a reviewer actually wants to see.

topics.title: What changed in agent security this quarter
topics.brief: Recurring quarterly piece. Compare the current corpus scan against the previous one from data/corpus-history.json: which rules became more or less prevalent, what that suggests. Only report a movement if the underlying counts support it — if the change is within a couple of repositories, say the data does not support a conclusion.
